articles.title: Yemen’s war is back: A new battle for Sanaa and the Red Sea
articles.summary: This phase of the war  could be the start of another protracted conflict rather than a decisive campaign, say analysts.
articles.body:
War is once again descending on Yemen, a country once described as the world’s worst humanitarian disaster.

The country is currently experiencing its most serious spell of fighting since 2022, when a United Nations-brokered truce halted eight years of a war that had killed tens of thousands of people.

This week, Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched counterattacks against the Houthi rebels, with fighting intensifying on Monday in the provinces of Taiz, al-Bayda and al-Jawf, the latter seen as one of the main gateways to the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa. The Houthis, meanwhile, say they have repelled some of the government forces’ advances and attacked Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government.

A wider landscape of regional instability and conflict has created new conditions for Yemen’s unresolved war to flare up once again.

Tensions escalated in July after government forces claimed an attack on the Houthi-controlled airport in Sanaa, preventing an aircraft from Iran from landing. More attacks followed, and it further escalated last week when the Houthis launched a major offensive, trying to advance through western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, towards the port city of al-Makha (Mocha) and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.

In this new phase of war, the internationally recognised government has its sights set on retaking the capital from the Iran-backed Houthis.

Both, meanwhile, are vying for control of the area near Bab al-Mandeb – which has gained greater significance amid Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz , a vital artery for global oil and gas supplies. The Houthis have conducted regular attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since 2023.

Analysts say that government-aligned forces are better resourced than at any point in the conflict, but they also warn against a swift victory.

“This is likely to be a protracted war rather than a rapid campaign,” Mohammed al-Basha, a Yemeni-American analyst and founder of Basha Report, a US-based risk advisory, told Al Jazeera.

Analysts say that the Yemeni government’s objective is to retake the whole of the country, after years of civil war and fragmented leadership.

Emboldened by its ability to take back areas in non-Houthi-controlled southern Yemen from the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a UAE-backed separatist group, earlier this year, the government is now setting its sights on the Houthis.

“The government was able to control more, and less militias [are] now on the ground … the only [other] player now [is the] Houthis in Sanaa,” Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of Middle East politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera.

Since the defeat of the STC, the Yemeni government has focused on presenting the country’s anti-Houthi forces as a united group with one military chain of command, after years of division.

Still, the Houthis remain a “formidable military force”, said al-Basha. “[The Houthis] are going to fight tooth and nail rather than simply fold.”

If the Iran-backed group is pushed back, it could dig into its northern tribal highlands around Saada, Hajjah, Sanaa and neighbouring governorates, said the analyst.

“That would create a much more geographically defined confrontation between a Houthi-held northern heartland and territories controlled by the internationally recognised government and its allies,” said al-Basha.

Against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran – and attacks from Iran and its allies on the Gulf – the opportunity has been ripe for the Saudi-backed Yemeni government to take on the Houthis.

“There is a wide perspective that non-state actors – militias – should be ended regionally,” said Zweiri, adding that there is growing aversion from regional states to such groups.

“This also is influencing what’s happening in Yemen,” he explained. “The government … [has] a green light to basically end the current status quo in Yemen.”

The US-Israel war on Iran is a particularly important catalyst, said Saudi political analyst Khaled Batarfi.

“The confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran has changed the strategic value of Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera. “The Houthis are no longer operating only within the framework of Yemen’s civil war; they have demonstrated an ability and willingness to connect the Yemeni battlefield with Red Sea security, international shipping and regional energy infrastructure.”

Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi territory – in which dozens of people have been wounded – are particularly significant, he added.

“They risk transforming the conflict again from an internal Yemeni confrontation into a direct Saudi-Houthi security crisis,” said Batarfi.

However, even if the wider confrontation involving Iran is resolved or de-escalated, “it does not necessarily follow that the Saudi-Houthi conflict will end”, said al-Basha.

“Yemen has its own unresolved war, its own territorial dynamics and its own political demands.”

How will this new phase impact regional heavyweights?

While Saudi Arabia and Iran appear to have an understanding aimed at preventing direct escalation, Iran-aligned armed groups – including the Houthis themselves – could work together to exert military and political pressure on Riyadh, said al-Basha.

The Houthis could impose “significant” costs on Saudi Arabia through coordinated long-range missile and drone attacks, even as they face increasing pressure on the ground, he said.

And while Saudi Arabia’s priority has been to prevent a return to an open-ended war in Yemen, “attacks on Saudi civilian and energy facilities inevitably change the calculation,” said Batarfi.

“No state can indefinitely tolerate direct attacks on its territory,” he said.

Iran, meanwhile, occupied with its war with the US, is limited by the additional support it can provide the Houthis, but will likely continue shipping missile and drone components, along with refined fuel and other commodities, said al-Basha.

Another key objective of the internationally recognised government has been to secure the Bab al-Mandeb Strait .

Iran is leveraging the Strait as a point of pressure through the Houthis, so one of the aims of the war is to ensure the waterway comes under the control of Yemen’s central government, Zweiri said.

That also partly explains Saudi Arabia’s support for the offensive – the Houthis had declared a blockade against Saudi vessels transiting the waterway, which is a vital corridor for shipping between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Bab al-Mandeb has even more significance for Saudi oil exports since Iran began restricting passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the US and Israel’s war on the country.

But the Houthis are also seeking an advance towards the vital Red Sea shipping route.

The group has demonstrated it possesses the firepower to threaten commercial and military shipping across the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and parts of the Arabian Sea, said al-Basha.

Eventually, they could also attempt to impose tolls in the waterway, mirroring Iran’s approach around the Strait of Hormuz, he added.

“If both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb become seriously disrupted at the same time, the consequences would extend far beyond Yemen or Saudi Arabia – it would become a major international energy and trade security problem,” said Batarfi.

The analysts were in agreement that the trajectory of the conflict appears to be heading towards a larger-scale war in the coming days.

“The government seems to be in a stronger position than at any time before, and it sees this round of fighting as an opportunity to consolidate its position and gain more territory from the Houthis,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst on Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

It is also the first time the government is fighting on more than one front, activating multiple arenas against the Houthis – and moving from a defensive position to an offensive one, he said. Government forces additionally are better coordinated and have access to more sophisticated weaponry than previous rounds, said Nagi.

It’s also likely a conflict that could drag on, said the analysts.

“Some initially expected a Syrian-style scenario, with Houthi defences unravelling rapidly in the way Bashar al-Assad’s regime collapsed,” al-Basha said, referring to the December 2024 lightning offensive that brought down al-Assad.

“If anything, what we may be looking at is closer to a Sudan-style scenario, with two relatively well-defined geographical blocs pitted against each other in a prolonged and costly conflict,” he warned.

articles.title: Boeing or Northrop Grumman? Pentagon nears decision on US Navy’s F/A-XX stealth fighter contract
articles.summary: International News: The Pentagon has decided which company will build the US Navy's next-generation stealth fighter and could announce the winner within the coming weeks .
articles.body: The Pentagon has decided which company will build the US Navy's next-generation stealth fighter and could announce the winner within the coming weeks or sooner, according to two people briefed on the matter, as reported by Reuters.Boeing and Northrop Grumman are competing for the contract, which previous programmes of similar scope suggest could be worth tens of billions of dollars over its lifetime.The programme, currently unnamed but designated F/A-XX, has faced years of delays and funding disputes. Some Pentagon officials had sought to postpone it by up to three years over concerns about engineering and supply chain capacity.However, Congress pushed back by allocating $750 million for F/A-XX in the major tax-cut and spending bill signed into law in 2025, followed by another $1.4 billion in fiscal 2026.A Pentagon spokesperson said, “We continue work to award the F/A-XX contract in the near future. There is no additional information at this time.”Navy's carrier fighter faces pressure from ChinaThe F/A-XX programme is moving forward as China rapidly fields advanced combat aircraft, including aircraft that Beijing describes as sixth-generation.The stakes of further delays are high, with the US Navy needing a modern fighter capable of operating from aircraft carriers in the 2030s and beyond. A US official has said delays could potentially undermine the Navy's ability to project power in contested environments.The carrier-borne fighter will be the centrepiece of the Navy's Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems.It is intended to replace the ageing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fleet, which has been in service since the 1990s. The F/A-18s are expected to remain in service into the 2040s.F/A-XX fighter expected in the 2030sThe new fighter is expected to feature advanced stealth capabilities, improved range and endurance, and the ability to integrate with uncrewed combat aircraft and the Navy's carrier-based air defence systems.The first production jets are expected to enter service in the 2030s.The Pentagon's selection of a contractor would mark a key step in the long-running F/A-XX programme, which has been affected by disputes over funding and the timing of its development.The contract is expected to be significant in value, with previous programmes of a similar scope suggesting a lifetime worth of tens of billions of dollars, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
articles.summary: The festival will return in June after taking a fallow year, but tickets have topped £400 for the first time.
articles.body:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page , organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website.

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Glastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.

The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.

Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.

Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.

In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85 - a 30% price hike.

The price hikes have multiple causes - from increased energy and infrastructure costs to post-Brexit labour shortages.

However, last weekend's Reading and Leeds festival held prices at their 2025 level, with passes costing £325, rising to £361 with early-bird entry.

Glastonbury said they would not be commenting on today's announcement but, in 2023, Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers.

"We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."

The festival last took place in 2025, with Olivia Rodrigo, The 1975 and Neil Young topping the bill.

Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis recently scotched rumours that Madonna would be among the headliners for next year's event.

"No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that," she told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show.

"But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well," she added.

Asked about the possibility of a performance from Taylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

articles.title: Meet Rachel Chen, the 18-year-old Los Angeles student who expanded a 1997 quantum-math idea to describe entire particle systems with simple diagrams; she won $100,000
articles.summary: US News: At just 18, Rachel Chen has taken a decades-old mathematical idea and expanded it into a visual framework for understanding complex quantum systems, e.
articles.body: At just 18, Rachel Chen has taken a decades-old mathematical idea and expanded it into a visual framework for understanding complex quantum systems, earning her a $100,000 award in the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search.Chen, a student at Marlborough School in Los Angeles, California, won fourth place in the prestigious competition for her mathematics project, titled The Dual Canonical Basis in the Spin Representation via the Temperley-Lieb Algebra.Her research builds on a 1997 mathematical finding involving Temperley-Lieb diagrams - simple point-and-curve illustrations that can be used to represent aspects of quantum systems.Chen's work extends that approach to describe how an entire system of quantum particles behaves under the influence of a magnetic field, potentially giving researchers a more intuitive way to examine relationships between different quantum-mechanical states.How Rachel Chen turned complex quantum physics into diagramsQuantum mechanics is notoriously difficult to represent mathematically because particles can interact with one another and their surroundings in complicated ways.Chen's project focuses on the spin representation, a mathematical framework used to describe the spin states of multiple particles.As she explains in her project presentation, a single electron has two possible spin states - up and down. Quantum superposition means that its state can be represented as a combination of those possibilities rather than simply one or the other.The mathematics becomes considerably more complicated when multiple electrons interact.Chen describes the spin representation of a system of n electrons using repeated tensor products of the complex plane, creating a structure that becomes increasingly difficult to visualise as the number of particles increases.Her research asks a deceptively simple question: Can that complicated mathematical structure be represented in a more visual and accessible way?Her answer involves the Temperley-Lieb algebra.What are Temperley-Lieb diagrams?Temperley-Lieb diagrams use points arranged along parallel lines and curves connecting those points.Although the diagrams look relatively simple, they can encode sophisticated mathematical relationships. According to Society for Science, researchers in mathematics and physics use Temperley-Lieb diagrams to study concepts including phase transitions and mathematical knots.Chen demonstrated that these diagrams can form a basis for the spin representation, effectively providing building blocks through which the complicated quantum system can be viewed.She went further by showing how the diagrams relate to a particularly important mathematical structure known as Lusztig's dual canonical basis.A new explicit formulaOne of the significant aspects of Chen's project was her work on the dual canonical basis.According to her presentation, there had previously been no explicit non-inductive formula for this basis of the spin representation.Using her diagrammatic approach, Chen developed what she described as the first explicit formula for the dual canonical basis of the spin representation.She also used the visual framework to revisit known classical results, demonstrating that the diagrammatic perspective was consistent with existing work before using it to derive new results.Her research additionally examined the Hecke algebra, a related mathematical object, and provided a new axiomatic description of the canonical basis of the spin representation.Making complicated quantum systems easier to visualiseThe potential importance of Chen's work lies not simply in creating attractive mathematical diagrams, but in using them to simplify the way researchers can think about highly complicated quantum structures.Society for Science said her approach could provide an intuitive framework for understanding the structure and connections among different quantum-mechanical states.Chen also extended the ideas from her project into additional work involving multiple-electron systems.In her presentation, she explained that her diagrams can be used to show explicitly how a system containing multiple electrons can decompose into multiple single-particle systems.That could provide another way to analyse complicated electron systems by breaking them down into simpler components.From mathematics competition to $100,000 awardChen's achievement came at the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search, one of the United States' most prominent competitions for high school seniors conducting original scientific research.The 2026 competition attracted more than 2,600 entrants, with 40 finalists competing for more than $1.8 million in awards.Chen ultimately secured fourth place and $100,000 for her research. The Society for Science specifically recognised her for developing a concrete, visual way to describe systems of many quantum particles using Temperley-Lieb diagrams and expanding on the 1997 finding.The top prize went to Connor Hill, while Chen ranked fourth among the 2026 finalists.Rachel Chen is also an internationally ranked chess playerChen's interests extend well beyond advanced mathematics and quantum physics.At Marlborough School, she founded the school's math club, which has grown to more than 100 members, and she plays volleyball.She is also an internationally ranked chess player and won her age group at the Pan-American Chess Festival in 2022. She serves as Contests Director for Athemath, a nonprofit focused on building a community for girls interested in mathematics.And despite working on highly complex mathematics, Chen has a decidedly pop-culture side: she is a devoted Taylor Swift fan and has memorised the words to more than 200 of the singer's songs.Her unusual combination of interests - from quantum mathematics and chess to volleyball and Taylor Swift - has helped make her one of the more distinctive young researchers recognised by this year's competition.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russell Layne found not guilty in connection to wife Emma Compton Layne’s 2017 death | Dateline
articles.summary: In 2024, Russell Layne was charged in connection to the 2017 death of his wife Emma Compton Layne. In September 2026, Layne was found not guilty of first-degree murder.
articles.body: On September 1, 2026, a jury in Halifax County, Virginia, found Russell Layne not guilty of first-degree murder in connection to the death of his wife, Emma Compton Layne, according to NBC affiliate WSLS. Dateline featured Emma’s story in October 2017. Emma vanished on Saturday, June 17, 2017, after she finished closing the convenience store she owned in Cody, Virginia, around 7:30 p.m. She was supposed to spend the following day at the hospital visiting her mother, but she never showed up. The family reported Emma missing that Tuesday, after they found Emma’s credit card, clothes, car keys, cell phone, and dog left behind at her home. Five months later, on November 22, 2017, hunters found human remains in the woods less than a mile from the property Emma and her husband owned. Major Tommy Spencer, of the Halifax County Sheriff’s Office, told NBC-affiliate WSLS at the time that the remains were scattered across the ground and someone seemed to have attempted to bury the body. “It appeared to have been in a very shallow grave,” Maj. Spencer said. The sheriff’s office suspected foul play upon finding the remains. According to a January 2018 press release by the Halifax County Sheriff’s Office, the remains were transported to the medical examiner’s office for autopsy, examination and positive identification. “We are still awaiting additional information from the medical examiner’s office concerning the circumstances and cause of death,” Sheriff Fred Clark said in the release. “But we are treating this as a homicide investigation and are continuing to pursue all possible leads related to Mrs. Layne’s death. This investigation is top priority.” In November 2024, the sheriff’s office posted on its Facebook page that Emma’s husband, Russell Wayne Layne, had been arrested for Emma’s death. He was charged with first-degree murder. Layne pleaded not guilty. On September 1, 2026, after seven days of hearing evidence and witness testimony, a jury found Layne not guilty of first-degree murder. Prosecutors alleged that based on security video, Layne was the only other person at the couple’s home at the time of the murder. His defense argued there was no direct evidence tying him to Emma’s death, according to WSLS. Commonwealth attorney Tracy Martin spoke to the media after the verdict. “My heart goes out to the family. I wish that it was different for them. I hope that they can take this chapter and use it to close the book and start to heal within themselves,” she told WSLS. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Bristol Airport delays sparked by air traffic control fault
articles.summary: Flights in and out of Bristol have been severely delayed by a nationwide air traffic control fault.
articles.body:
Flights have been cancelled and delayed at Bristol Airport amid UK-wide technical issues affecting air traffic control.

Stranded passengers have complained of long delays, with the airport's live departures page showing dozens of flights either cancelled or with "estimated" departure times far later than originally scheduled.

Air traffic control group Nats said earlier a "technical issue" was affecting flights departing the UK . A fix was underway they later added, but the problem has caused extensive disruption to flight schedules.

Bristol Airport has advised passengers to check their flight information with their airline before heading to the airport.

Nessie Robertson, 64, who was due to fly from Menorca to Bristol with her elderly parents, told the BBC she expected to be stranded for six hours.

"We were due to board at 17:00 BST but nobody turned up at the gate to let us through," Robertson said.

"My husband who is in the UK texted to tell me that there was an issue with air traffic control.

"So far we have been told we would be delayed for two hours hours, then six hours - my parents are 90 and 88."

Lisa Jacobson, 50, said her daughter was due to fly from Bristol to Faro at 13:30, but had been grounded for more than five hours.

Others took to social media to report being stuck overseas, including in Crete and Venice.

In its initial statement, Bristol Airport said the issue was only impacting departures, before clarifying arrivals were also being delayed.

"We recommend passengers travelling today to contact their airline directly to check the latest flight information and prior to leaving for the airport," a spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for Nats said: "We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system. Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible.

"Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time."

In an update shared late on Tuesday evening, Bristol Airport said disruption was "likely to continue" into Wednesday.

articles.title: Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US revives Ukraine peace efforts
articles.summary: The phone call comes after US special envoys travelled to Russia and Ukraine to discuss ‘a proposal to end the war’.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has spoken by phone with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin as the White House ramps up efforts to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Yury Ushakov, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, described the two leaders as having a “constructive and quite frank” hour-long conversation.

According to Ushakov, Putin talked with Trump about the ongoing war in Ukraine and Russia’s plans to advance its military goals on the battlefield.

“An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation’s goals and tasks was given,” Ushakov said.

The adviser added that Putin pushed back against rising concern that Russia could launch future attacks in Europe, including on NATO members.

“It was underlined that we don’t have any aggressive plans regarding Europe,” Ushakov said.

The White House did not return Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the reported call.

The phone call comes just days after US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss what Trump has described as “a proposal to end the war”, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.

Ushakov told reporters Putin and Trump “exchanged views on the outcome of the visits”, saying some “very good, worthwhile ideas” were presented.

After his Sunday meeting with the US envoys concluded, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for “allowing them to come” to Ukraine, despite the ongoing fighting, which was briefly paused for the negotiations.

“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said.

“To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.

The meetings, despite being lauded by all sides, appeared to produce no breakthrough on ending the fighting. After the brief weekend truce, both countries resumed strikes.

Officials in Ukraine said Russian attacks on Tuesday morning killed at least five civilians and wounded 25 others in Kyiv.

Meanwhile, Russian officials reported three people killed in the Bryansk and Kursk regions, with 13 others wounded. Ukrainian attacks on Russian-annexed Crimea also killed approximately five people, according to local authorities.

The war began in February 2022, after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, considered the breadbasket of Europe.

Trump has made ending the war a priority of his second administration, pledging on the campaign trail that he could achieve a settlement within 24 hours.

He later backtracked on that claim, calling it an exaggeration. Faced with reports that certain US munitions stocks are dwindling, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine for putting a drain on the country’s missile supplies and finances — though critics point to US actions against Iran as a major factor.

While Trump has had a rocky relationship with Ukraine and its president, he has cultivated a close relationship with Putin, saying they went through “a hell of a lot” together.

Last year, Trump invited him to Alaska for his first visit on US soil since 2015.

The Trump administration has faced criticism for seeking to end the war in Ukraine without fully involving Ukrainian and European officials. Trump and Zelenskyy are expected to meet later in the month, according to Ukrainian officials.

articles.title: China and Qatar are strengthening bilateral ties: What that really means
articles.summary: Beijing says it will increase coordination with Doha to help de-escalate regional tensions amid the ongoing war on Iran.
articles.body:
Beijing, China – Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani has completed a two-day visit to China, with officials describing the relationship as entering a new “golden decade”.

China has called Qatar an “important strategic partner” in the Middle East and the Gulf, and the two sides have agreed to expand cooperation in energy, investment and advanced technologies.

But it’s clear the continuing US-Israeli war on Iran, and ongoing Qatari efforts to mediate between Tehran and Washington, were central to discussions.

“It’s not acceptable at all to have this state of no war and no peace. This is not beneficial to the region, the countries of the region, and the people,” Ibrahim bin Sultan al-Hashmi, director of the Department of Media and Communications at Qatar’s Foreign Ministry, told reporters in Doha on Tuesday following the meetings. “Qatar is working hard with its partners, including China. Diplomatic efforts are being exerted and new ideas are being discussed.”

Beijing pledged to increase communication and coordination with Doha to help restore regional peace and stability. Qatar has told China it would prioritise its energy supply despite the difficulties.

The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has raised the stakes for both sides.

Qatar is one of the world’s biggest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG), while China is the world’s largest importer of crude oil. Both have a significant interest in restoring stability to the strait, through which around one-fifth of global oil and LNG normally passes.

Energy is also the backbone of the relationship. China is Qatar’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade worth $23.8bn last year. Qatar is China’s second-largest source of LNG, supplying 19.4 million tonnes in 2025. QatarEnergy has signed 27-year LNG supply agreements with Chinese state-owned energy giants CNPC and Sinopec, which have also taken stakes in Qatar’s massive North Field gas expansion.

Overlapping interests, different approaches

But despite these shared interests, Doha and Beijing have different ways of dealing with Tehran.

China has repeatedly voiced support for Qatar’s mediation efforts but has largely refrained from direct criticism of Tehran’s attacks or its disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. It’s also consistently placed primary blame for the conflict on the US and Israel, a conflict Chinese officials say “never should have happened”.

Beijing is arguably Tehran’s most important economic and diplomatic partner . China has for years been the largest buyer of its oil and continues to oppose unilateral sanctions against it .

During talks with Al Thani, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi repeated calls for a diplomatic solution, saying “pressure exerted through military means is not a solution; dialogue and negotiations are the only viable path”.

For its part, Qatar has publicly condemned Tehran for attacks on its own territory and on neighbouring Gulf states. It has grown increasingly frustrated with failed or stalled attempts to resolve the crisis, while continuing to facilitate dialogue.

From Doha’s perspective, closer coordination with Beijing potentially brings another influential player into its efforts to end the conflict, one with unusually strong economic and political ties to Tehran.

China is also aware of Qatar’s longstanding security and military partnership with Washington, Beijing’s biggest strategic rival.

Qatar hosts Al Udeid, the largest US military base in the Middle East. On March 3, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at Qatar. One was intercepted while the other struck Al Udeid, causing no casualties. This prompted Doha to call for even stronger security ties with Washington.

Still, China has no interest in replacing the US as a security guarantor, says Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow at the Center for China and Globalization in Beijing. “What we are seeing is Beijing positioning itself as a relevant political and economic actor at a moment when several states in the region are looking for additional options,” Khan said.

The question is how much of its own influence Beijing is prepared to use when it comes to Iran. China has so far shown little appetite for using its leverage to exert significant pressure on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The Qatari prime minister’s two-day visit was, of course, about more than Iran. If anything, the conflict has increased the incentive for Doha and Beijing to expand their relationship towards what Qatar has described as “broader horizons”. China’s Premier Li Qiang called for deeper cooperation in traditional and renewable energy, infrastructure, artificial intelligence and finance, while Al Thani singled out high technology and advanced manufacturing.

Invest Qatar reports that 520 Chinese companies operate in the country, with Chinese investment projects generating more than $3bn and creating more than 3,200 jobs this past decade.

The visit underlines a partnership that is becoming broader economically, and potentially more important diplomatically, as the Iran war tests both countries’ ability to protect the interests that bind them together.

articles.title: Ladakh's tourist footfall continues rising; August sees most foreign visitors
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: Ladakh has recorded a sharp rise in tourist arrivals this year, with 4,05,085 visiting the Union Territory in the first eight months of 2026.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Ladakh has recorded a sharp rise in tourist arrivals this year, with 4,05,085 visiting the Union Territory in the first eight months of 2026, exceeding the 3,35,872 tourists recorded for all of 2025. “In just eight months of 2026, the total tourist footfall has exceeded by 20.6% from the total tourist arrivals recorded in 2025,” a govt spokesperson said.Aug 2026 saw the highest foreign tourist footfall recorded in any month so far this year, with 10,075 foreigners travelling to Ladakh. “This is also considerably higher than the 8,148 foreign tourists recorded in Aug 2025,” the spokesperson said.The growth was recorded across both domestic and foreign tourist segments. “During the first eight months of 2026, Ladakh received 3,71,739 domestic tourists and 33,346 foreign tourists, compared to 2,44,308 domestic and 25,082 foreign tourists during the corresponding period in 2025,” the spokesperson said.In Aug, major festivals like Changthang Nomadic Festival, the first-ever Black-necked Crane Festival, Suru Summer Festival, and Ladakh Book Festival added new attractions to Ladakh’s tourism calendar and attracted a huge number of tourists, the spokesperson said. “The first edition of Black-Necked Crane Festival alone saw the participation of more than 10,000 people from India and abroad. These festivals showcase Ladakh region’s unique culture, nomadic traditions, wildlife and natural heritage,” he added.Ladakh’s tourism calendar remains active in Sept as well, with a series of major events lined up, including Ladakh Bike Week, Ladakh Festival, Zanskar festival, and the Ladakh Marathon, the spokesperson said. “The marathon, in particular, attracts runners from across the country and beyond, with many participants travelling to Ladakh with their families, thereby generating wider benefits for hotels, homestays, restaurants, transport operators, guides, local businesses and other tourism-related services,” he added.Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena attributed the growth to central govt’s sustained push for infrastructure development in Ladakh, as well as PM Narendra Modi’s appeal to citizens to visit locations in India and promote domestic tourism.“The fact that Ladakh has already crossed its entire 2025 tourist footfall in just eight months of this year is a very encouraging sign. Our focus, however, is not merely on increasing tourist numbers but on building a sustainable, responsible and year-round tourism economy that benefits our people,” Saxena said. articles.title: In 1971, a surfer cut a piece of foam with an electric carving knife; 55 years later, his invention is a household name
articles.summary: US News: A leftover piece of foam, an electric carving knife, and a surfer were all Tom Morey needed to create what would become one of surfing’s most recognis.
articles.body: A leftover piece of foam, an electric carving knife, and a surfer were all Tom Morey needed to create what would become one of surfing’s most recognisable inventions. In 1971, Morey was living in Kona, Hawaii, where he was experimenting with the idea of a small and lightweight craft that could offer a different way to ride waves. He was already an accomplished stand-up surfer, but he kept looking for new possibilities.According to the California Surf Museum, Morey took a piece of polyethylene foam from his garage and cut it into shape with an electric carving knife. He then used his wife’s iron to seal the foam. A copy of the Honolulu Advertiser newspaper left its imprint on the board, giving Morey a way to remember the date: July 7, 1971. That simple experiment would go on to become the Morey Boogie and help shape the modern bodyboard.How Tom Morey created the first modern bodyboardMorey’s creation was different from the hard surfboards he knew. The modern bodyboard was a soft and flexible piece of foam designed to be ridden while lying on the belly. Morey found that the board allowed him to feel the movement of the wave in a way that a conventional surfboard did not. He saw several advantages in his new creation. It could turn, was durable and lightweight, and could be produced cheaply. Morey also believed it was safe. The idea was simple enough to turn into a do-it-yourself kit that people could assemble at home.The first kits came with two pieces of foam that had to be glued together along with skins for the top and bottom. Morey placed an advertisement in Surfer magazine, and orders soon began arriving.From a garage experiment to the Morey BoogieMorey initially considered calling his invention SNAKE (Side, Navel, Arm, Knee, and Elbow). The name was an acronym for the parts of the body used while riding it. But the idea was rejected, and he eventually chose the name Morey Boogie.The name came from Morey’s love of jazz and a style of swing music which was popular before the Second World War. He felt that ‘Boogie’ captured the movement of the new craft.The first production of the Morey Boogie reached the market in 1975. By 1977, the Carlsbad-based company was producing about 80,000 boards a year. In 1979, toy company Kransco purchased Morey Boogie, and the boards began appearing in major department stores across the United States.Why the Boogie Board name still lives onMorey’s invention helped establish modern bodyboarding as a sport. By the 1980s, bodyboarding had become the fastest-growing watersport in the world, according to the California Surf Museum.Today, many companies make their own versions of the bodyboard. Yet the name Morey has proved that it is difficult to replace. The museum notes that people still commonly call bodyboards ‘Boogie boards', much as brand names such as Band-Aid, Coke, Kleenex and Vaseline have become part of everyday language.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first post-colonial leader, dies at 89
articles.summary: Hong Kong ‘s first post-handover leader, Tung Chee-hwa, who struggled to cope with an Asian financial crisis and democracy protests, has died at 89.
articles.body: Hong Kong ‘s first post-handover leader, Tung Chee-hwa, who struggled to cope with an Asian financial crisis and growing protests for democracy in the early years under Chinese rule, has died at age 89. His office said in a statement that Tung passed away peacefully in the presence of his family members on Tuesday. Tung, a shipping tycoon, had little political experience before a panel of pro-Beijing elites picked him in 1997 to be the first leader of the southern Chinese territory after the end of British colonial rule. Many believe Beijing perceived Tung as a loyalist who would obey the Communist leadership’s edicts. He was also seen as beholden to Beijing because China’s state-run banks helped rescue his family’s ailing shipping company — Orient Overseas Container Line — during a global slump in the 1980s. The early years after the handover were sensitive. The “one country, two systems” formula, in which Hong Kong was supposed to maintain civil liberties and other remnants of its British past while Beijing had the final say on issues such as political change, was still untested. Tung was praised for his work ethic, even nicknamed “7-11” because of his reputation for long workdays, but clumsy political skills and perceived indecisiveness as major crises mounted eroded his popularity and led to a less flattering nickname, “Old Dumb Tung.” Shortly after Tung took office in 1997, Hong Kong was hit by bird flu — the first known cases of the virus in humans. The wealthy city’s economy was also battered by a financial crisis that swept across Asia. Tung’s response to the two crises was widely criticized and his deep distrust of the media hindered his ability to improve his image. He was also prone to policy gaffes that made him the butt of jokes. Despite his rocky first term, Tung was reelected unopposed by the pro-Beijing electoral committee in 2002. A year later, Tung faced another serious test when SARS — severe acute respiratory syndrome — hit Hong Kong, killing nearly 300 people and devastating the economy. Tung’s government was accused of a sloppy, sluggish response. Later in 2003, Tung gained more critics by proposing an anti-subversion law, locally known as Article 23 legislation. Many saw it as a threat to civil liberties, and an estimated half million people joined a street march against it. The government later scrapped the legislation. Hong Kongers held another massive protest in 2004 to demand direct elections for the city’s leader and the entire legislature. Tung sided with China’s communist leaders, who rejected it, and the rally became an annual event for pro-democracy supporters for years. The large-scale protests might have signaled to Beijing that the Hong Kong public was becoming more politically divided and that Tung was losing control. He confirmed he was leaving on March 10, 2005, insisting his failing health was the reason, not pressure from Beijing. “If I continue as chief executive, I won’t be able to handle it,” he said. Many were suspicious about Tung’s explanation because no health problems were apparent in the months before his resignation. Tung was born in Shanghai on May 29, 1937, and his family moved to Hong Kong in 1947, two years before the Communists took over the mainland. After earning a degree in marine engineering from the University of Liverpool in 1960, Tung worked for General Electric and his family’s shipping company in the United States before returning to Hong Kong in 1969. He started a think tank after leaving the city’s top job and remained a Beijing loyalist during major protests for democracy in 2019 and an ensuing crackdown on dissent in which the central government imposed a national security law on the city that outlawed subversion. As the protests raged in September 2019, he was among 42 people who received national medals and honors from Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a ceremony in Beijing for their contributions to the country. Tung was recognized for devoting himself to the implementation of the “one country, two systems” policy. Following the enactment of the security law in 2020, massive protests that once challenged Tung’s leadership vanished in the city. Tung has not been seen at public events over the past several years.

articles.title: Lincolnshire County Council to object to major solar farm plan
articles.summary: Meridian Solar Farm Limited is seeking permission to build a solar farm near Spalding.
articles.body:
A council has agreed to formally object to plans for a huge solar farm on Lincolnshire farmland.

Meridian Solar Farm Limited is seeking permission for a 40-year development consent order to build a solar farm on about 2,700 acres (1,092 hectares) of land near Spalding.

At a Lincolnshire County Council meeting on Monday, councillors described the plans as a "large-scale industrialisation" of the countryside and an example of "greed".

However, David Vernon, from Meridian Solar Farm Limited, said the project would "provide domestic, renewable energy at a time when it is most needed".

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the solar farm would have a peak generation capacity of 750MW, which would be transferred to Weston Marsh Substation B - which is not yet built - by a fresh set of pylons.

Councillor Martin Hill said: "They're already putting an application in before they've even got a connection - which tells you of the undue speed and haste and greed."

Councillor James Bean said, until the Weston Marsh substation is in place, there would be no guarantee the project would be deliverable.

Councillors were told there are 13 public rights of way either partially or fully within the proposed project area.

Bean added: "This is not a small-scale site, but a large-scale industrialisation of productive green land over a huge area of Lincolnshire.

"When considered in conjunction with other solar projects in Lincolnshire, this constitutes an overburden on Lincolnshire residents for national benefit."

Vernon said: "The Meridian Solar Farm project will make a significant contribution to energy security in the UK, providing energy for up to 215,000 homes each year."

He said it was "critical" Meridian Solar Farm and other large-scale renewable projects were progressed "to ensure the clean energy projects contribute to the national need as soon as practicable".

Vernon said the company had worked closely with Lincolnshire County Council on its proposals.

"Across multiple rounds of consultation, we have sought to take on board their views and feedback where possible," he added.

The solar farm is classed as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), which means the decision to allow it will be determined by the government, rather than a local council.

The plans are currently undergoing examination by the Planning Inspectorate. Hearings took place on Tuesday.

The council will make its representation to the secretary of state in which it will recommend to the government that the application should be refused.

articles.title: Jerry Sandusky, former Penn State coach convicted of sex abuse, seeks new trial after victim recants
articles.summary: Former Penn State football coach Jerry Sandusky is seeking a new trial in federal court after one of his accusers recanted.
articles.body: Disgraced former Penn State football coach Jerry Sandusky appeared virtually in court on Tuesday and told a judge he understood his legal team’s move in seeking a new trial in federal court after one of his accusers recanted. Tainted victim testimony led to Sandusky’s wrongful conviction for child sexual abuse, according to his lawyers, who believe their client’s best chances for freedom now come from moving the case from the Pennsylvania system to a U.S. courthouse. But in moving this case to another court, Sandusky’s legal team surrenders its right to litigate in state court claims that Victim No. 10, identified in court papers as “R.R.,” was allegedly manipulated into misleading testimony. Sandusky, 82, an inmate at State Correctional Institution (SCI) Laurel Highland serving a term of at least 30 years, was convicted after multiple young men testified they were sexually abused by the former assistant coach as boys. Sandusky used his good name in the community and his nonprofit, The Second Mile, to meet victims, prosecutors have said. Judge Maureen Skerda asked Sandusky, who appeared via video feed from prison, if he understood his legal team’s actions and he confirmed that he did. “I’m making this decision on advice of counsel,” Sandusky said, according to the Associated Press. Judge Skerda later ruled that “the Court being satisfied that Mr. Sandusky has been fully informed of his rights and understood Counsel’s action in withdrawing the claim concerning R.R.’s recantation, the Court hereby” dismisses the coach’s state court bid for post-conviction relief. His appellate attorneys claim that damaging testimony from several alleged victims have been subsequently shown to be problematic, particularly Victim 10, “R.R.” That victim came forward with “new evidence” on June 30, 2025, that he had been “approached by state investigators who told me that my role was critical to stopping a predator,” according to Sandusky’s defense team. Prosecutors told Victim 10 “other alleged victims were reluctant to come forward and repeatedly encouraged me to believe that Mr. Sandusky had molested me-despite my lack of clear or certain memory of any such conduct,” according to the recanting witness has said, Sandusky’s lawyers have said. “I was told — both directly and indirectly — that trauma may have fragmented my memory, and that I could safely affirm details I did not fully recall. I was assured this was common and even expected,” according to a statement from R.R. Sandusky’s attorney claimed that “R.R. maintained that his account changed over time as ‘the result of emotional strain, repeated exposure to leading questions, intense investigative pressure and psychological manipulation.’ ” Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday called Sandusky a “child predator” and dismissed the coach’s legal maneuvers. “This was yet another attempt by a convicted child predator to avoid accountability and escape punishment for years of abuse he perpetrated under the veil of a child-empowerment program,” AG Sunday said in statement on Tuesday afternoon. “I commend our litigation team for challenging this alleged recantation by one victim, and putting on record the voluminous evidence that debunks this highly-suspect claim by defense counsel.” Sandusky was convicted on June 22, 2012, on 45 sex abuse-related counts and then sentenced to 30 to 60 years behind bars. The scandal led to Penn State firing Sandusky’s boss, legendary coach Joe Paterno, for his alleged failure to take appropriate action against the longtime defensive coordinator. A statue of Paterno, who led the Nittany Lions went 409-136-3 in 46 seasons on the Penn State sideline, was removed from the football stadium in the midst of the Sandusky reckoning. But in the years since the scandal and Paterno’s death, the coach’s supporters have gained traction in re-evaluating his legacy. The university recently opened the “Paterno Family Football Experience Room” inside Beaver Stadium, calling it a “permanent museum experience celebrating more than a century of Penn State Football history.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. articles.title: US warns Americans about exit bans and 'unjust' detention in popular destination
articles.summary: The U.S. State Department is warning Americans traveling to China about exit bans, arbitrary detention and surveillance of private electronic messages.
articles.body: Americans who may be planning a trip to China are urged to take extra precautions, as U.S. officials warn travelers to "keep a low profile" while visiting the country. The State Department recently updated its Level 2 "Exercise Increased Caution" advisory for mainland China, warning Americans about the arbitrary enforcement of local laws, exit bans and "the risk of unjust arrest or detention." U.S. citizens could be questioned or detained without being told what crime they are accused of — and without being given access to U.S. consular services, according to the advisory. AMERICANS HEADED FOR HIGH-RISK NATION URGED TO PREPARE WILLS, LEAVE DNA SAMPLES AHEAD OF TIME "U.S. citizens in China may also face interrogations and detention without fair and transparent treatment under the law," the State Department warns. The advisory notes that business people, academics and journalists are among those who have faced questioning, detention or expulsion for alleged violations of China's national security laws. "U.S. citizens might only become aware of an exit ban when they attempt to depart China," the advisory states. The State Department said the restrictions have been used to pressure people to participate in investigations, resolve civil disputes and compel relatives or associates to return to China. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES In some cases, exit bans have remained in place for years, preventing U.S. citizens from leaving the country even to receive medical treatment, according to the advisory. Officials are also warning Americans to be careful about what they say and share electronically while traveling. "Assume that China's security services can read your emails, texts, and social media posts if you send them to or from China," the advisory states. The State Department warns that Americans could be detained or deported for private electronic messages critical of China, Hong Kong, Macau or the Chinese Communist Party. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Authorities have detained people over messages sent while they were outside China, according to the advisory. For Americans who decide to travel to mainland China, officials recommend avoiding demonstrations and being cautious around large gatherings. Travelers are also advised to avoid sharing opinions either publicly or privately that Chinese authorities could consider embarrassing or negative and to avoid photographing protesters or police without permission. "Keep a low profile," the State Department advises. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The updated advisory also includes separate guidance for Hong Kong and Macau. Americans are advised to exercise increased caution in Hong Kong due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws. Macau carries a higher Level 3 "Reconsider Travel" advisory due to similar concerns and the U.S. government's limited ability to provide emergency consular services there. articles.title: India, Japan to conduct two-week air exercise Veer Guardian 2026 in Jodhpur from today
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Indian Air Force (IAF) and Japan Air Self Defence Force (JASDF) will conduct bilateral Air Exercise, Veer Guardian-2026, at Air Force S.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Air Force (IAF) and Japan Air Self Defence Force (JASDF) will conduct bilateral Air Exercise, Veer Guardian-2026, at Air Force Station Jodhpur, from Wednesday till Sept 22, the defence ministry said on Tuesday.The 14-day exercise will see the participation of frontline fighter aircraft from both countries. While the Indian Air Force will participate with a diverse mix of frontline combat aircraft, including indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas, Su-30 MKl and Rafale jets, JASDF will participate with its F-2A fighter aircraft, the ministry said.The Japanese F-2A is a close cousin of the American F-16 Fighting Falcon, sharing the same basic airframe design but heavily modified for maritime defence. The participation of Japan’s F-2A fighter jets in Veer Guardian-2026 will give the IAF a valuable opportunity to train against a close relative of the F-16.The exercise will provide an opportunity to the air warriors of both India and Japan to undertake advanced operational missions and enhance interoperability through extensive professional interactions.During the exercise, participating air warriors will undertake advanced operational missions and engage in extensive professional interactions. The program integrates mission planning conferences, subject matter expert exchanges, and interaction between personnel on engineering and aspects of aerospace safety, fostering deep operational synergy between the two air forces.Exercise Veer Guardian-26 reflects a deepening strategic partnership between India and Japan by enhancing tactical proficiency and aerospace operational synergy. The exercise reaffirms the longstanding bonds of friendship and strategic cooperation between the two nations.

articles.title: Iran launched another attack on US navy ships Monday, with fears of China, Russia aid: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran launched an attack targeting US navy ships on Monday, but the US military has not yet acknowledged the incident, the Wall Street Journal reported.
articles.body: Iran launched an attack targeting US navy ships on Monday, but the US military has not yet acknowledged the incident, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials. The reported attack came after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer over the weekend.No US navy ships were hit in the attacks, according to the officials.However, the repeated attempts to target American warships have raised concerns that Iran may be using more advanced weapons and could be receiving help from China or Russia.The attacks also show that Iran is taking a more aggressive approach as a US blockade of Iranian ports puts further pressure on its economy. The moves could increase tensions, as the US has warned it will respond to attacks on its navy vessels.After Iran tried to target a US aircraft carrier over the weekend, the US struck three Iranian oil tankers. Washington said the tankers were helping fund Iran’s military and proxy groups. US officials said the strikes were intended to make clear that attacks on American warships would not be tolerated.Iranian state media has claimed that the country is using new missiles with advanced technology to target US warships. According to weapons analysts, these missiles could be equipped with electro-optical seekers, allowing them to use images to adjust their path toward moving targets.However, Iran would still need to know roughly where US warships are located before launching an attack. This has raised concerns among US officials that China or Russia could be helping Iran track American naval vessels.Iran unveiled the Qassem Bassir, a medium-range ballistic missile equipped with such seeker technology, last year, according to John Caves, a senior research associate at the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control. He said other Iranian missiles, including the Khalij Fars, also use the technology.The US hopes its blockade and sanctions will put enough pressure on Iran to force its leadership to back down. articles.title: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
articles.summary: Israel's response to London's trade ban with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank shows how important this moment is.
articles.body:
Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.

Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.

Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.

The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.

They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.

Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.

For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.

Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.

Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.

And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.

As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.

That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this and worse," is truly remarkable.

Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.

Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.

Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment.

But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.

Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.

But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.

For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress.

The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".

In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".

Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.

The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.

Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.

In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.

But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.

Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.

So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

articles.summary: Former Obama aides on "Pod Save America" appeared to joke about heart disease and time catching up to President Donald Trump, sparking fierce backlash.
articles.body: Former Obama aides who host the "Pod Save America" podcast appeared to joke on Tuesday about President Donald Trump dying of heart disease or old age. Co-host and former Obama speechwriter Jon Favreau read questions from their audience, opening with one that asked, "'Is there anyone that can stop this orange piece of s---?!!!’ Three exclamation points. Vanessa from Facebook," referring to Trump. "I just thought I'd put that one first because that's just a tenor of the questions we get from Facebook." "Iran's doing a pretty good job. So far," Tommy Vietor, another former Obama aide, replied. "I think the answer is no," Favreau said. 'POD SAVE AMERICA' ACCUSED OF TEMPORARILY DELETING CLIP CRITICAL OF PIKER AFTER EX-BIDEN STAFFER AMPLIFIED IT "Heart disease has always got a shot," Vietor quipped. "Father Time will get there eventually." Jon Lovett, who had been a speechwriter for both Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, observed, "The hardness of the veins sort of gets us all in the end." "Anyway, you know, it's 2026, almost 2027, so pretty soon we won't be asking that question," Favreau concluded. "Then what happens?" co-host and former Obama communications director Dan Pfeiffer asked. "We then get real jobs?" "Probably," Favreau suggested. MARK HAMILL POSTS PHOTO DEPICTING DEAD TRUMP JUST DAYS AFTER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, told Fox News Digital that the conversation was a grim sign of the times. "Democrats are increasingly a post-American political movement," he said. "There used to be shared American societal standards that meant speculating publicly on a president’s death was crass and inappropriate, and those are gone now. And in its place is the attitude of anything — even violence — that advances my preferred policies is good. In any event, the president is vigorous and in command of his office, something that couldn’t have been said about President Biden." "Four men who once worked steps from the Oval Office sat around mics betting on which will claim the sitting president first — heart disease, 'Father Time' or hardened veins — and not one of them had the decency to flinch," Morgan Murphy, a former Pentagon press secretary, told Fox News Digital. "Favreau admitted the quiet part himself: that's 'just the tenor' of what their audience sends in, which tells you this ghoulishness isn't a slip of the tongue on the Left anymore — it's the signature of today’s Democrats," he continued. articles.title: Man accused of midair racist outburst loses job after duct-tape flight to Newark
articles.summary: The man accused of delivering an erratic outburst aboard a flight bound for Newark Airport has lost his job after photos showed the unusual method used to restrain him.
articles.body: The man accused of delivering an erratic outburst aboard a flight bound for Newark Airport has lost his job after photos showed the unusual method used to restrain him. Arthur Lundeen, of Arizona, reportedly became disruptive on American Airlines Flight 618, which boarded in Dallas, and multiple passengers had to help duct tape him his seat. Lundeen was arrested by authorities in Maryland after flight was diverted. Lundeen was a real estate agent with Long Realty in Tuscon and has since been fired from the company, NBC affiliate KVOA reported. “Upon learning of the incident, Long Realty promptly ended its affiliation with the individual,” Long Reality said, in part, in a lengthy statement posted on Facebook. “The individual is no longer associated with or authorized to represent Long Realty in any capacity. The 67-year-old is facing disorderly conduct and assault charges. Contact information for his attorney was not immediately known. Two men who work in Woodland Park, New Jersey, witnessed the midair outburst firsthand and jumped into action to help the flight attendants on board. Richard O’Lenick and Juan Mejia, a former police officer, said Lundeen was shouting racial and homophobic slurs before he started to get physical. “The flight attendants tried to de-escalate him. They were just getting spit venom from him, derogatory remarks, racial comments,” Mejia said. “So I said to him, if he escalates from there, I’m going to have to get involved.” The pair said flight attendants first pulled out zipties, before resorting to duct tape. Mejia said he grabbed the tape and went to work. “I didn’t cover his eyes, I didn’t cover his airways — his nose, his mouth — that was the most important thing. We’re not looking to hurt the gentleman but we’re looking that he doesn’t hurt himself any further, or us or anyone else,” O’Lenick explained. “I’m glad that we were able to do what we did,” O’Lenick added. The airline released a statement saying “the safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority.”

articles.title: Man pleads not guilty to misdemeanor charges in Ohio fair incident involving Amy Acton
articles.summary: A man accused of knocking an elderly couple to the ground in an attempt to confront Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton on Sunday has pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from the incident.
articles.body: A man accused of knocking an elderly couple to the ground in an attempt to confront Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton on Sunday has pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from the incident. Patrick Havas, 38, appeared via video in Mahoning County on Tuesday to face two charges of assault, one charge of disorderly conduct, and one charge of inducing panic. He entered a plea of not guilty to all charges. Acton, a Democrat, was visiting the annual Canfield Fair in Canfield on Sunday afternoon when the incident occurred. Havas allegedly pushed his way through a crowd in an attempt to approach Acton, knocking two elderly individuals over in the process, according to an incident report obtained by NBC News on Tuesday. Ohio state troopers working as Acton’s security detail grabbed Havas as he attempted to approach her, the report said. Law enforcement officials reported finding two handguns, a set of brass knuckles and a Taser on Havas after arresting him. Havas never brandished a weapon during the incident, the incident report said. A judge agreed to a $5,000 cash surety bond for Havas and ordered him to surrender any weapons he owns as a condition of the bond. Havas was also instructed to not speak to media and to have no contact with the elderly couple and Acton following his release. Havas’ attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment following Tuesday’s hearing. Records show that Havas was previously arrested in 2008 on a charge of petty theft. He pleaded no contest and the charge was reduced to disorderly conduct. Mahoning County Prosecutor Lynn Maro defended her office’s decision not to pursue felony charges against Havas after Tuesday’s hearing. She noted that Havas never made physical contact with Acton or brandished a weapon. Adults are allowed to possess a firearm without a permit under Ohio’s open-carry law so long as they are not concealed under clothing. Maro told reporters that there were no charges that would fit “for simply possession of those weapons.” “We’re not going to let emotions take over,” Maro said. “We’re going to follow the evidence. We’re going to follow the facts, and that’s how we’re going to prosecute.” Acton’s campaign had asked for people to stop recording shortly before the incident, Maro said, but Havas was recording at the time. Havas consented to a “complete search” of his phone, according to Maro. Prosecutors have video from his vantage point, which Maro said does not support a pursuit of felony charges. “It shows him walking into the tent, recording, and moving forward, calling out her name ... Somebody in her security comes forward, and then his phone is either dropped or tousled, and that’s all we have,” Maro said. Acton described it as a “rough day” during a Labor Day parade in Cleveland on Monday, according to NBC News affiliate WKYC. She expressed gratitude to those who helped the injured individuals and the state troopers who provided security. “I am a fierce warrior in this fight,” Acton said. “That’s exactly why I’m running. I refuse to look the other way like people didn’t look the other way when I was a struggling kid in Youngstown, Ohio. I won’t look the other way, and you are refusing to look the other way.” Three witnesses to the incident told NBC News that they saw the suspect knock two older attendees to the ground. They also saw Acton, a physician, help care for them in the aftermath. The individuals names were redacted from the incident report and NBC News was unable to reach them for comment on Tuesday. They were treated on scene and released, the report said. Former Rep. John Boccieri, D-Ohio, said he was within an “arm’s length” of acton and that Havas made it “within feet” of the gubernatorial candidate. He described the incident as “an aggressive move from a very large man.” “He was yelling, ‘Dr. Acton! Dr. Acton!’” Boccieri said. “And when the State Highway Patrol and the security detail grabbed him, he said, ‘I was just trying to ask a question.”
